summary: The NX 450h+ is the only plug-in hybrid in the Lexus NX range — the far more common NX 350h is a conventional hybrid with no plug — and it pairs an 18.1kWh (gross) battery with a 2.5-litre petrol four for 227kW and all-wheel drive. Its distinguishing trait is that it stays frugal once the battery is flat: the European WLTP battery-empty figure is 6.4L/100km and Australian testers record about 5.4-6.0L/100km, where most European PHEVs of this size drink 8L/100km or more. Reviewers rate the refinement, build and the $84,630 Luxury grade, but are consistently critical of the $96,090 F Sport's value against cheaper plug-in rivals, the 6.6kW AC-only charging with no DC option, and an 87km local range claim that is NEDC-derived and above the 72km European WLTP figure — and a facelifted NX with a bigger battery and DC charging is due in the first half of 2027.
pros: Charge-sustaining economy is genuinely low for a 2.05-tonne premium SUV: Chasing Cars measured about 6.0L/100km running on petrol alone with the battery depleted over a ~1000km long-term test, and CarExpert saw 5.7L/100km across a mostly-highway week — so an owner who cannot plug in still gets Toyota hybrid consumption rather than the 8-9L/100km typical of European PHEVs

The NX450h+ Luxury AWD at $84,630 before on-road costs is $11,460 cheaper than the $96,090 F Sport that was previously the only way into the plug-in drivetrain, and it keeps the same 18.1kWh battery, 227kW output and e-Four all-wheel drive as the flagship

Lexus Australia's five-year, unlimited-kilometre warranty is unconditional, and the hybrid battery carries separate 10-year unlimited-kilometre cover that can be extended a further 10 years through annual health checks at a Lexus dealer

Boot space is not sacrificed to the plug-in hardware — the battery sits under the cabin floor, so the 450h+ keeps the same 520-litre boot (1141L seats folded) as the NX 350h hybrid, unlike the Kia Sorento PHEV and Mazda CX-60 PHEV which both lose volume to their packs

Real-world electric range is usable rather than token: Australian testers report 53-70km on a full charge, enough for a typical Melbourne commute, and the car will hold EV mode to 135km/h rather than firing the engine at highway speeds
cons: Charging is AC-only at a maximum 6.6kW with no DC fast-charge capability at all, and the supplied cable is a 10A domestic lead that CarsGuide timed at roughly six hours for 35-100 per cent — a buyer without a home wallbox has no practical way to keep the battery full, at which point the car is simply an expensive NX 350h

The advertised 87km electric range is an NEDC-derived figure on the Australian energy label; the current European WLTP figure is 72km, so the headline number overstates the range by roughly 20 per cent before real-world driving is considered — Australian testers saw 53-60km from a full charge

The 1.3L/100km label consumption is meaningless in normal use — the WLTP battery-empty figure is 6.4L/100km, EV Central measured 5.4L/100km and CarExpert 5.7L/100km — and the car requires 95 RON premium unleaded, so the fuel bill is roughly four times what the sticker implies

At $96,090 before on-roads the F Sport sits above the $91,661 fuel-efficient luxury car tax threshold and draws direct comparison with the Audi Q5 and BMW X3; EV Central scored it 3/5 on the basis that it is 'just not that rare or special any more' against Chinese plug-in hybrids costing $40,000-$60,000 less

The current car is about to be superseded: CarExpert reports a facelifted NX450h+ with a roughly 23kWh battery, a 100km-plus WLTP range claim and DC fast charging due in Australian showrooms in the first half of 2027, and braked towing on today's car is capped at 1000kg against 1500kg-plus for most rivals
